title: Job 1 — The bnei-elohim council and the first test

paragraphs.text: אִ֛ישׁ הָיָ֥ה בְאֶֽרֶץ־ע֖וּץ אִיּ֣וֹב שְׁמ֑וֹ וְהָיָ֣ה ׀ הָאִ֣ישׁ הַה֗וּא תָּ֧ם וְיָשָׁ֛ר וִירֵ֥א אֱלֹהִ֖ים וְסָ֥ר מֵרָֽע׃

i18n.en: A man there was in the land of Uz, Job by name; and that man was blameless and upright, one who feared Elohim and turned from evil.

notes.official: **The book opens outside Israel.** *Eretz Uz* — *the land of Uz* — is identified in Gen 10:23 as descended from Aram (Shem's line), and in Gen 22:21 as Nahor's eldest son. The location is generally placed east of the Jordan, possibly in northern Arabia or Edom (Lam 4:21 locates 'the daughter of Edom dwelling in the land of Uz'). The chapter is staging Job's story **outside Israel** — among the Aramean / Edomite peripheries, in a non-Israelite cultural sphere. // *Iyov* (אִיּוֹב) — *Job*. The name's etymology is contested. Possible derivations: (1) from a root meaning *the hated / persecuted one* (cognate with Akkadian *ayyabu* — enemy); (2) from *ayyeh-ab* — *where is the father*; (3) an Amorite or West Semitic personal name with no obvious etymology. The chapter offers no folk etymology — unlike most Hebrew Bible introductions of named figures, Job's name is given without a wordplay. // *Tam v'yashar* — *blameless and upright*. *Tam* is from *tom* (completeness, integrity, wholeness — not 'perfect' in the moral-absolute sense but unblemished/whole in the ritual sense). *Yashar* (upright, straight) is the ethical-conduct twin. The pair recurs in 1:8, 2:3 as YHWH's own characterization of Job. // *Yere Elohim v'sar me-ra* — *feared Elohim and turned from evil*. The chapter is positioning Job in the **Wisdom-literature register** — *yir'at Elohim* (fear of Elohim) is the canonical Wisdom virtue (Prov 1:7, 9:10, 15:33). The chapter is announcing this is a Wisdom-book even before the dialogue starts.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּוָּ֥לְדוּ ל֛וֹ שִׁבְעָ֥ה בָנִ֖ים וְשָׁל֥וֹשׁ בָּנֽוֹת׃

i18n.en: Seven sons and three daughters were born to him.

notes.official: **The numbers are symbolic.** Seven sons + three daughters = ten children. Seven is the number of completeness; three is the number of formal-ritual structure; ten is the number of plenitude. The chapter is signaling Job's life as *complete* by the canonical symbolic numerology. The same numbers will recur at 42:13 in the restoration: seven sons, three daughters (the children Job is given after his ordeal). The book's symmetry-by-numbers is structural.

paragraphs.text: וַיְהִ֣י מִ֠קְנֵהוּ שִֽׁבְעַ֨ת אַלְפֵי־צֹ֜אן וּשְׁלֹ֧שֶׁת אַלְפֵ֣י גְמַלִּ֗ים וַחֲמֵ֨שׁ מֵא֤וֹת צֶֽמֶד־בָּקָר֙ וַחֲמֵ֣שׁ מֵא֣וֹת אֲתוֹנ֔וֹת וַעֲבֻדָּ֖ה רַבָּ֣ה מְאֹ֑ד וַיְהִי֙ הָאִ֣ישׁ הַה֔וּא גָּד֖וֹל מִכָּל־בְּנֵי־קֶֽדֶם׃

i18n.en: His livestock numbered seven thousand sheep, three thousand camels, five hundred yoke of cattle, and five hundred donkeys, with very many servants — and that man was greater than all the sons of the east.

notes.official: **Job's wealth itemized.** The numbers are pastoral-archetypal: seven thousand sheep, three thousand camels — the doubled seven/three pattern recurs. The chapter is establishing Job's wealth in the canonical Wisdom-narrative register: not a king (no land or political power named), but a *pastoralist* of the eastern peripheries. // *Bnei qedem* — *sons of the east* — names the eastern Aramean/Edomite pastoral peoples; Job is the *greatest* among them. The chapter is staging Job as a regional patriarch in the same sociological register as the Genesis patriarchs (Abraham, Isaac, Jacob) — though geographically east of the Jordan rather than in Canaan.

paragraphs.text: וְהָלְכ֤וּ בָנָיו֙ וְעָשׂ֣וּ מִשְׁתֶּ֔ה בֵּ֖ית אִ֣ישׁ יוֹמ֑וֹ וְשָׁלְח֗וּ וְקָרְאוּ֙ לִשְׁל֣שֶׁת אַחְיֹתֵיהֶ֔ם לֶאֱכֹ֥ל וְלִשְׁתּ֖וֹת עִמָּהֶֽם׃

i18n.en: His sons used to go and hold a feast in each one's house on his day; and they would send and call for their three sisters to eat and drink with them.

paragraphs.text: וַיְהִ֡י כִּ֣י הִקִּיפֽוּ֩ יְמֵ֨י הַמִּשְׁתֶּ֜ה וַיִּשְׁלַ֧ח אִיּ֣וֹב וַֽיְקַדְּשֵׁ֗ם וְהִשְׁכִּ֣ים בַּבֹּקֶר֮ וְהֶעֱלָ֣ה עֹלוֹת֮ מִסְפַּ֣ר כֻּלָּם֒ כִּ֚י אָמַ֣ר אִיּ֔וֹב אוּלַי֙ חָטְא֣וּ בָנַ֔י וּבֵרֲכ֥וּ אֱלֹהִ֖ים בִּלְבָבָ֑ם כָּ֛כָה יַעֲשֶׂ֥ה אִיּ֖וֹב כָּל־הַיָּמִֽים׃

i18n.en: When the days of the feast had run their cycle, Job would send and consecrate them, rising early in the morning and offering whole burnt offerings according to the number of all of them — for Job said, "Perhaps my children have sinned and have blessed Elohim in their hearts." Thus Job did all the days.

notes.official: ***Berakhu Elohim*** — literally *blessed Elohim*, but here the chapter is using the verb *barakh* as a **euphemism for *curse***. The reverential-substitution device is well-attested in the Hebrew Bible: when the text needs to put curse-language next to *Elohim* or *YHWH*, it uses the opposite verb *barakh* (bless) instead. The substitution recurs in this chapter at 1:11 (the satan's prediction: 'he will *bless you*' = 'he will curse you to your face') and at 2:5, 2:9. The scribal-euphemistic device makes the meaning clear from context — Job is anxious that his children might have *cursed* Elohim, not that they blessed him. // The chapter is opening with Job's preemptive intercession on his children's behalf — he is a priestly-figure, offering *olot* (whole burnt offerings) for them, *misper kullam* (according to the number of all of them, individually). The verb *kiddesh* (sanctify, consecrate) is the cultic-purification action. Job functions as priest for his household, in a way that anticipates the Aaronic priesthood but precedes it textually.

paragraphs.text: וַיְהִ֣י הַיּ֔וֹם וַיָּבֹ֙אוּ֙ בְּנֵ֣י הָאֱלֹהִ֔ים לְהִתְיַצֵּ֖ב עַל־יְהוָ֑ה וַיָּב֥וֹא גַֽם־הַשָּׂטָ֖ן בְּתוֹכָֽם׃

i18n.en: The day came when the sons of the Elohim came to present themselves before YHWH — and the adversary also came among them.

notes.official: **The book's keystone scene.** *Vay'hi ha-yom* — *the day came* — opens the heavenly-council scene. // *Bnei ha-elohim* — *sons of the Elohim* — the same plural-class divine-council figures named in Gen 6:2-4 and Ps 82:6, 89:6-7 (cf. glossary entry [`b-nei-ha-elohim`](/wiki/sons-of-elohim/)). The chapter is staging a **periodic council assembly**: the *bnei ha-elohim* come *l'hityatzev al-YHWH* — *to present themselves before YHWH*. The verb *yatzav* in hithpael denotes formal-ritual presentation for inspection or duty (cf. Num 11:16 of the seventy elders, 1 Sam 10:19, 2 Chr 11:13). The bnei-ha-elohim are *court members* presenting themselves to their sovereign. // ***Ha-satan*** (הַשָּׂטָן) — *the adversary*. The Hebrew preserves the definite article *ha* — making this **a functional role, not a proper name**. *Ha-satan* is *the satan*, *the adversary* — a member of the divine council whose role is adversarial-prosecutorial. The same role-noun appears in 1 Chr 21:1 (where *satan* lacks the article and is read by some as a proper name), in Zech 3:1-2 (*ha-satan* standing at the right hand of the high priest Joshua to accuse him), and in Num 22:22, 32 (where YHWH's *malakh* stands as a *satan* — adversary — in Balaam's path). // The KJV/ASV rendering 'Satan' (capitalized, proper-noun) is a Christian-tradition retrojection. The figure of *Satan-the-devil* in later Christian theology is built up over centuries from disparate sources (the serpent of Gen 3, the morning-star of Isa 14, the dragon of Rev 12); the Hebrew Bible's *ha-satan* in Job 1-2 is a council-member with permission to test, not the personified evil-deity. // The WoH translation preserves the Hebrew article — **'the adversary'** — matching the modern scholarly consensus (NJPS, Clines's Anchor Bible commentary, Habel's OTL, Newsom in NIB). The translation does not commit to the proper-name reading; the commentary surfaces the role-vs.-personified-deity question. // *Va-yavo gam ha-satan b'tokham* — *and the adversary also came among them*. The verse positions ha-satan **as one of the bnei-ha-elohim** — among them, presumably *one of them*. The chapter is staging adversarial-prosecution as a *function* internal to the divine council, not an external evil counterforce.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֧אמֶר יְהוָ֛ה אֶל־הַשָּׂטָ֖ן מֵאַ֣יִן תָּבֹ֑א וַיַּ֨עַן הַשָּׂטָ֤ן אֶת־יְהוָה֙ וַיֹּאמַ֔ר מִשּׁ֣וּט בָּאָ֔רֶץ וּמֵֽהִתְהַלֵּ֖ךְ בָּֽהּ׃

i18n.en: YHWH said to the adversary, "From where do you come?" And the adversary answered YHWH and said, "From roaming the earth and walking back and forth on it."

notes.official: ***Shut ba-aretz u-me-hithallekh bah*** — *from roaming the earth and walking back and forth on it*. Two verbs of locomotion: *shut* (rove, range) and *hithallekh* (walk-about). // The hithpael *mithallekh* is the chapter's most pointed lexical echo. The same verbal form is used of YHWH-Elohim *walking about* in the garden (Gen 3:8), of Enoch *walking about* with the Elohim (Gen 5:22, 24), of Noah *walking about* with the Elohim (Gen 6:9). The verb denotes habitual, at-home movement-in-residence. // Ha-satan walks-about *on the earth* — in the same verbal form as the patriarchs walked-about *with the Elohim*. The chapter is positioning ha-satan as having the earth as its movement-domain in the same way the antediluvian-favored figures had divine company as theirs. The role is *territorial-investigative*: ha-satan ranges the earth, presumably collecting information for the council. The function is **prosecutorial** — an inspector or examiner — not metaphysically-evil. // The chapter does not give ha-satan an explicit job-description. The Hebrew Bible elsewhere implies the role: in Zech 3 ha-satan stands as legal accuser; in Num 22 the malakh-as-satan blocks Balaam. Ha-satan in Job 1-2 ranges the earth, comes to council, and is queried about its findings. The function-set is *adversarial-prosecutor-and-inspector*.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר יְהוָה֙ אֶל־הַשָּׂטָ֔ן הֲשַׂ֥מְתָּ לִבְּךָ֖ עַל־עַבְדִּ֣י אִיּ֑וֹב כִּ֣י אֵ֤ין כָּמֹ֙הוּ֙ בָּאָ֔רֶץ אִ֣ישׁ תָּ֧ם וְיָשָׁ֛ר יְרֵ֥א אֱלֹהִ֖ים וְסָ֥ר מֵרָֽע׃

i18n.en: YHWH said to the adversary, "Have you set your heart on my servant Job? For there is none like him on the earth — a man blameless and upright, one who fears Elohim and turns from evil."

notes.official: **YHWH initiates the topic of Job.** *Hasamta libekha al-avdi Iyov* — *have you set your heart on my servant Job?* The phrase *sim lev al* (set heart upon) means *give attention to, focus on, scrutinize*. YHWH is asking whether ha-satan has noticed Job specifically. // *Avdi* — *my servant* — is the canonical Hebrew Bible designation for figures of singular divine-relational status: Moses (*avdi Moshe*, Num 12:7-8, Deut 34:5, Josh 1:2), David (*avdi David*, 2 Sam 7:5, 1 Kgs 11:13), the Isaianic Suffering Servant (Isa 52:13). Job is now named in the same register. The chapter is positioning Job as a figure of high covenantal status — *YHWH's servant*, of singular-exemplary character. // YHWH's recitation of Job's characterization — *tam v'yashar yere Elohim v'sar me-ra* — is identical to the narrator's at 1:1. The divine voice and the narrator's voice agree: Job is what he is said to be. // The chapter is structurally setting up the test: YHWH points out Job; ha-satan will challenge the basis of Job's righteousness. The challenge is not over Job's *piety* (no one disputes that) but over its *motivation* (transactional vs. unconditional).

paragraphs.text: וַיַּ֧עַן הַשָּׂטָ֛ן אֶת־יְהוָ֖ה וַיֹּאמַ֑ר הַֽחִנָּ֔ם יָרֵ֥א אִיּ֖וֹב אֱלֹהִֽים׃

i18n.en: The adversary answered YHWH and said, "Does Job fear Elohim for nothing?"

notes.official: **The adversary's challenge.** ***Ha-chinnam yare Iyov Elohim*** — *does Job fear Elohim for nothing / freely?* The crucial word is *chinnam* (חִנָּם) — *for nothing, gratis, without compensation, without cause*. The adverb appears in Gen 29:15 (Laban: 'should you serve me *for nothing*?'), Ex 21:2 (the freed slave goes out *chinnam*, without payment), Num 11:5 (the fish 'we ate in Egypt *chinnam*' — without cost). // Ha-satan's challenge is precisely-targeted: the question is not whether Job is righteous but whether his righteousness is *transactional*. The accusation: Job worships because Job is paid to (with wealth, children, security). Remove the payment — the argument runs — and the worship collapses. // The argument is **technically interesting**. It assumes that worship-without-reward would be the genuine article, and worship-with-reward is merely paid behavior. The chapter is staging the question of *motivation* as the test. // *Chinnam* will return through the book as a keyword. Job himself in 2:3 will be called *gratuitous* — *t'sitheni vo l'val'o chinnam* — *you incited me against him to swallow him without cause*.

paragraphs.text: הֲלֹֽא־את [אַ֠תָּה] שַׂ֣כְתָּ בַעֲד֧וֹ וּבְעַד־בֵּית֛וֹ וּבְעַ֥ד כָּל־אֲשֶׁר־ל֖וֹ מִסָּבִ֑יב מַעֲשֵׂ֤ה יָדָיו֙ בֵּרַ֔כְתָּ וּמִקְנֵ֖הוּ פָּרַ֥ץ בָּאָֽרֶץ׃

i18n.en: Have you not put a hedge around him and around his house and around all that is his on every side? You have blessed the work of his hands, and his livestock has spread out in the land.

notes.official: **The adversary's evidence.** Ha-satan lays out the case: YHWH has hedged Job in (*sakhta ba'ado* — the verb *sakhakh* covers *enclose, screen, protect*). The hedge is comprehensive: around Job, around his house, around everything he has. YHWH has *blessed* (*berakhta*) the work of Job's hands and *spread out* (*paratz*) his livestock. // The verse reads as a divine cost-benefit summary: YHWH has invested heavily in Job's prosperity. The adversary's implicit argument: *no wonder he's pious — look at the deal you've given him*. // Ketiv/qere note: the text has *at* (אַת — second-person feminine singular pronoun) as ketiv; the masoretic vocalization is *attah* (אַתָּה — second-person masculine singular) as qere. The chapter accepts the qere reading addressed to YHWH.

paragraphs.text: וְאוּלָם֙ שְֽׁלַֽח־נָ֣א יָֽדְךָ֔ וְגַ֖ע בְּכָל־אֲשֶׁר־ל֑וֹ אִם־לֹ֥א עַל־פָּנֶ֖יךָ יְבָרֲכֶֽךָּ׃

i18n.en: But put out your hand and touch all that is his — and surely he will curse you to your face.

notes.official: **The proposed test.** *Shelach-na yadekha v'ga b'khol-asher-lo* — *put out your hand and touch all that is his*. *Naga* (*touch*) is the chapter's understatement-verb for the catastrophic disasters of vv 13-19 — to *touch* is to bring devastating loss. // *Im-lo al-panekha y'varakhekka* — literally *if not to your face he will bless you*. The Hebrew uses the strong oath-formula *im-lo* — equivalent to *surely* — and the verb *barakh* (bless) as the **euphemism for curse** (cf. commentary at 1:5). The adversary's prediction in plain language: *he will curse you to your face*. // The chapter is restating its central wager precisely. The adversary's case: remove the hedge, and the worship reverses. YHWH's confidence: Job's piety is unconditional.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר יְהוָ֜ה אֶל־הַשָּׂטָ֗ן הִנֵּ֤ה כָל־אֲשֶׁר־לוֹ֙ בְּיָדֶ֔ךָ רַ֣ק אֵלָ֔יו אַל־תִּשְׁלַ֖ח יָדֶ֑ךָ וַיֵּצֵא֙ הַשָּׂטָ֔ן מֵעִ֖ם פְּנֵ֥י יְהוָֽה׃

i18n.en: YHWH said to the adversary, "Behold, all that he has is in your hand — only against him do not put out your hand." And the adversary went out from before YHWH.

notes.official: **The permission and its limit.** *Kol asher-lo b'yadkha* — *all that he has is in your hand*. The adversary is granted **delegated authority** over Job's possessions and household. The limit: *raq elav al-tishlach yadkha* — *only against him do not put out your hand* — Job himself is exempt from the first test. // The chapter is making the structure of authority explicit: ha-satan acts under YHWH's permission, within boundaries YHWH sets. This is the strongest textual datum against the later Christian Satan-the-devil reading: ha-satan in Job 1 is neither autonomous nor opposed to YHWH; ha-satan operates *within YHWH's delegated authority*, bound by YHWH's specified limits. The function is *adversarial* (testing, accusing) but not *adversarial-to-YHWH*. // *Va-yetze ha-satan me-im pnei YHWH* — *and the adversary went out from before YHWH*. The council scene ends; the test begins.

paragraphs.text: וַיְהִ֖י הַיּ֑וֹם וּבָנָ֨יו וּבְנֹתָ֤יו אֹֽכְלִים֙ וְשֹׁתִ֣ים יַ֔יִן בְּבֵ֖ית אֲחִיהֶ֥ם הַבְּכֽוֹר׃

i18n.en: The day came when his sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in the house of their oldest brother;

notes.official: **The disaster sequence begins.** *Vay'hi ha-yom* — *the day came* — the same chapter-formula as 1:6 (the council scene). The chapter is staging the disasters on a *day* that the family was celebrating — making the loss specific and dated. // The next four verses (vv 14-19) form a tight quartet: four disasters reported in four parallel-structured messenger-arrival sequences, with the same closing formula *va-imal'tah raq ani l'vadi l'haggid lakh* — *and I alone have escaped to tell you*.

paragraphs.text: וּמַלְאָ֛ךְ בָּ֥א אֶל־אִיּ֖וֹב וַיֹּאמַ֑ר הַבָּקָר֙ הָי֣וּ חֹֽרְשׁ֔וֹת וְהָאֲתֹנ֖וֹת רֹע֥וֹת עַל־יְדֵיהֶֽם׃

i18n.en: A messenger came to Job and said, "The oxen were plowing and the donkeys were grazing beside them,

paragraphs.text: וַתִּפֹּ֤ל שְׁבָא֙ וַתִּקָּחֵ֔ם וְאֶת־הַנְּעָרִ֖ים הִכּ֣וּ לְפִי־חָ֑רֶב וָֽאִמָּ֨לְטָ֧ה רַק־אֲנִ֛י לְבַדִּ֖י לְהַגִּ֥יד לָֽךְ׃

i18n.en: when Sheba fell upon them and took them, and they struck down the young men with the edge of the sword. I alone have escaped to tell you."

notes.official: **First disaster: Sheba raiders.** *Sheba* (שְׁבָא) — the southern Arabian kingdom (Saba) named in Gen 10:7 (Cushite branch) and Gen 10:28 (Joktanite branch). The chapter is reporting a southern-Arabian raid on Job's livestock. The first disaster is *human-causal* — a raid by a named people.

paragraphs.text: ע֣וֹד ׀ זֶ֣ה מְדַבֵּ֗ר וְזֶה֮ בָּ֣א וַיֹּאמַר֒ אֵ֣שׁ אֱלֹהִ֗ים נָֽפְלָה֙ מִן־הַשָּׁמַ֔יִם וַתִּבְעַ֥ר בַּצֹּ֛אן וּבַנְּעָרִ֖ים וַתֹּאכְלֵ֑ם וָאִמָּ֨לְטָ֧ה רַק־אֲנִ֛י לְבַדִּ֖י לְהַגִּ֥יד לָֽךְ׃

i18n.en: While this one was still speaking, another came and said, "Fire of Elohim fell from the skies and burned up the sheep and the young men and consumed them. I alone have escaped to tell you."

notes.official: **Second disaster: *esh Elohim* from the skies.** *Esh Elohim nafelah min ha-shamayim* — *fire of Elohim fell from the skies*. The expression is striking. *Esh Elohim* (fire of Elohim) is a recurring Hebrew Bible designation for **divinely-sent fire** — lightning, supernatural conflagration. The same phrase appears at 2 Kgs 1:12 (the fire that consumes the captains of fifties before Elijah). // The lens reads the verse with attention: *fire from the skies* (literal lightning or atmospheric-electrical phenomenon) burned the flock and shepherds. The chapter is naming a *meteorological-disaster* in technical-cosmological vocabulary. // The disasters are escalating in agent-type: first human (Sheba raiders), now sky-fire. The pattern will continue: a third human-attack (Kasdim raiders, v17), then a wind-disaster (v19).

paragraphs.text: ע֣וֹד ׀ זֶ֣ה מְדַבֵּ֗ר וְזֶה֮ בָּ֣א וַיֹּאמַר֒ כַּשְׂדִּ֞ים שָׂ֣מוּ ׀ שְׁלֹשָׁ֣ה רָאשִׁ֗ים וַֽיִּפְשְׁט֤וּ עַל־הַגְּמַלִּים֙ וַיִּקָּח֔וּם וְאֶת־הַנְּעָרִ֖ים הִכּ֣וּ לְפִי־חָ֑רֶב וָאִמָּ֨לְטָ֧ה רַק־אֲנִ֛י לְבַדִּ֖י לְהַגִּ֥יד לָֽךְ׃

i18n.en: While this one was still speaking, another came and said, "The Kasdim formed three columns and raided the camels and took them, and they struck down the young men with the edge of the sword. I alone have escaped to tell you."

notes.official: **Third disaster: Kasdim raiders.** *Kasdim* — same people as named in Gen 11:28 (Ur Kasdim) and Ezek 1:3 (eretz Kasdim) — the Aramean-tribal people who became the Neo-Babylonian dynasty in the first millennium BCE. In Job 1:17 they are raiders, not yet imperial. The *shloshah rashim* (three columns) is military-tactical vocabulary — a coordinated raid in three contingents. // The book is set early (the patriarchal-archaic register the chapter has established at v3); the Kasdim appearance is anachronistic with that early setting but consistent with the chapter's broader chronological-mixing (cf. *Ur Kasdim* in Gen 11). The chapter is treating the Kasdim as a generic raiding-Aramean people without committing to a specific historical period.

paragraphs.text: עַ֚ד זֶ֣ה מְדַבֵּ֔ר וְזֶ֖ה בָּ֣א וַיֹּאמַ֑ר בָּנֶ֨יךָ וּבְנוֹתֶ֤יךָ אֹֽכְלִים֙ וְשֹׁתִ֣ים יַ֔יִן בְּבֵ֖ית אֲחִיהֶ֥ם הַבְּכֽוֹר׃

i18n.en: While this one was still speaking, another came and said, "Your sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in the house of their oldest brother,

paragraphs.text: וְהִנֵּה֩ ר֨וּחַ גְּדוֹלָ֜ה בָּ֣אָה ׀ מֵעֵ֣בֶר הַמִּדְבָּ֗ר וַיִּגַּע֙ בְּאַרְבַּע֙ פִּנּ֣וֹת הַבַּ֔יִת וַיִּפֹּ֥ל עַל־הַנְּעָרִ֖ים וַיָּמ֑וּתוּ וָאִמָּ֨לְטָ֧ה רַק־אֲנִ֛י לְבַדִּ֖י לְהַגִּ֥יד לָֽךְ׃

i18n.en: and behold, a great wind came from beyond the desert and struck the four corners of the house — and it fell on the young people, and they died. I alone have escaped to tell you."

notes.official: **Fourth disaster: a great wind from beyond the desert.** *Ruach gedolah ba'ah me-ever ha-midbar* — *a great wind came from beyond the desert*. The verb *naga* (touch, strike) names the wind's action — it *struck* the four corners of the house. // The wind is described as a single-event localized phenomenon: it came from across the desert, struck the house at all four corners simultaneously, brought the house down on the occupants. The combination of *coming from beyond the desert*, *striking simultaneously at four points*, and *causing total structural collapse* fits a strong wind-event (possibly a downburst or strong khamsin-style desert windstorm). // The four disasters together: Sheba raid, sky-fire, Kasdim raid, desert windstorm. Two human (1, 3), two natural (2, 4) — but the natural ones are described in divine-causal vocabulary (*esh Elohim* and *ruach gedolah*). The chapter is staging the disasters as having both human and natural-meteorological agents, with all four under ha-satan's delegated authority.

paragraphs.text: וַיָּ֤קָם אִיּוֹב֙ וַיִּקְרַ֣ע אֶת־מְעִל֔וֹ וַיָּ֖גָז אֶת־רֹאשׁ֑וֹ וַיִּפֹּ֥ל אַ֖רְצָה וַיִּשְׁתָּֽחוּ׃

i18n.en: Job arose, tore his robe, sheared his head, fell to the ground, and worshipped.

notes.official: **Three mourning-actions, then worship.** *Qara me'il* (tore his robe), *gazaz rosh* (sheared/shaved his head), *nafal artzah* (fell to the ground). These are the standard Hebrew Bible mourning rites (cf. Gen 37:34, 2 Sam 13:31, Ezra 9:3, Mic 1:16). Then *yishtachu* — *worshipped* — the standard verb for prostration-in-worship. // The verb-sequence is precise. Job mourns by the standard rites, but then *worships*. He does what one does when one has lost everything — and then orients toward YHWH. The chapter is staging the response that vv 21-22 will explicitly name: not curse but blessing-in-the-strict-sense.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּאמֶר֩ עָרֹ֨ם יצתי [יָצָ֜אתִי] מִבֶּ֣טֶן אִמִּ֗י וְעָרֹם֙ אָשׁ֣וּב שָׁ֔מָה יְהוָ֣ה נָתַ֔ן וַֽיהוָ֖ה לָקָ֑ח יְהִ֛י שֵׁ֥ם יְהוָ֖ה מְבֹרָֽךְ׃

i18n.en: And he said, "Naked I came forth from my mother's womb, and naked I shall return there. YHWH gave, and YHWH has taken; may the name of YHWH be blessed."

notes.official: **The book's most-quoted line.** *YHWH natan v'YHWH laqach — y'hi shem YHWH m'vorakh* — *YHWH gave and YHWH has taken — may the name of YHWH be blessed*. The two clauses are perfectly balanced: the same verb-class (*natan* — give, *laqach* — take), the same divine subject (YHWH), the opposite actions. // The chapter's keystone theological-claim: Job acknowledges that the same agent who *gave* now *takes*. The acknowledgment is unconditional — neither the giving nor the taking changes Job's orientation. The response *y'hi shem YHWH m'vorakh* — *may the name of YHWH be blessed* — uses *barakh* in its **strict-positive sense** (here genuinely *blessed*, not the euphemism-for-curse of v5, v11). The verse is the precise inverse of the adversary's prediction (v11): the adversary expected Job to *curse* (using *barakh* as euphemism); Job actually *blesses* (using *barakh* in its strict sense). // *Arom mi-beten immi* — *naked from my mother's womb*. The naked-came-naked-go formula picks up the universal-mortality acknowledgment (cf. Eccl 5:14 — 'naked he came from his mother's womb, and naked he shall return as he came'). The chapter is invoking the common-human-condition register: Job does not claim special-Job-status; he speaks as a *human* who came-and-will-go in the universal condition. // *Ketiv/qere note*: *yatsati* (qere) for *yatsa-ti* (ketiv) — the personal-affixed form vs. the simpler form.

paragraphs.text: בְּכָל־זֹ֖את לֹא־חָטָ֣א אִיּ֑וֹב וְלֹא־נָתַ֥ן תִּפְלָ֖ה לֵאלֹהִֽים׃

i18n.en: In all this Job did not sin, nor did he charge Elohim with anything unseemly.

notes.official: **The first test's verdict.** *Lo chata Iyov v'lo natan tiflah l'Elohim* — *Job did not sin, nor did he charge Elohim with anything unseemly*. // The verb *chata* (sin, miss-the-mark) is in its standard cultic-ethical register. *Tiflah* (תִּפְלָה) is a hapax-style noun from a root *tafel* (unsavoury, insipid, foolish) — denoting *something distasteful* or *something improperly directed*. Job did not *put unsavoury speech* against Elohim. // The verse is the chapter's narrator-judgment: Job passed the first test. The verse closes the chapter; the next chapter will open with a second council scene and a second, escalated test. The adversary's wager has lost round one.
